body:
Why do plants need transport tissues?

Roots absorb water and mineral nutrients from the soil, while leaves prepare organic food through photosynthesis. These substances must reach growing and other living parts of the plant, including regions that cannot photosynthesise.

Plants have specialised conducting tissues called xylem and phloem. Together, they form an important part of the plant's vascular system.

Xylem transports water and minerals

Xylem conducts water and dissolved mineral nutrients from the roots to the stem, leaves and other parts of the plant. Its conducting elements include vessels and tracheids. These form pathways through which water can move over considerable distances.

Water entering the roots reaches the xylem. The upward movement of water is assisted by root pressure and, particularly in tall plants, by the pull generated when water evaporates from leaves.

Transpiration produces an upward pull

Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from aerial parts of plants, mainly through leaf stomata. When water evaporates from leaf surfaces, it helps create a pulling force on the continuous water column within the xylem. This is called transpiration pull.

Transpiration also helps cool plant surfaces. However, excessive water loss can be harmful when soil water is limited, so stomatal opening is regulated by guard cells.

Phloem transports prepared food

Phloem transports products of photosynthesis, particularly dissolved sugars such as sucrose, from regions where they are available to regions where they are needed or stored. This movement is called translocation.

For example, sugars made in mature leaves may be transported towards growing shoots, roots, fruits or storage organs. Food can also move from a storage organ towards a growing part when the plant requires it.

Phloem contains conducting elements such as sieve tubes, which function with companion cells in flowering plants. Loading substances into phloem may require energy in the form of ATP.

Unlike the usual upward movement of water in xylem, food movement through phloem can occur upwards or downwards, depending on the location of the source and the part requiring the food.

Xylem and phloem compared

FeatureXylemPhloem
Principal substances transportedWater and dissolved mineralsProducts of photosynthesis, mainly sugars
Typical directionMainly roots towards upper partsFrom sources to regions of use or storage
Conducting elementsVessels and tracheidsSieve tubes and associated cells
Principal driving processTranspiration pull, aided by root pressureMovement driven by pressure differences established through food loading and unloading

Prelims focus

  • Xylem transports water and minerals.
  • Phloem transports products of photosynthesis.
  • Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, especially through stomata.
  • Transpiration pull helps water rise through xylem.
  • Phloem translocation can occur towards growing or storage regions above or below a source.
  • Trap: Phloem transport is not necessarily restricted to a downward direction.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.4.2, pp. 94–95, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, “Transportation in Animals and Plants”, pp. 128–131, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 6, “Tissues”, pp. 71–72, 2018–19 printing.]

pictures.caption: Water loss through leaves helps pull water upwards through xylem.

title: Transportation in Plants: Xylem, Phloem and Transpiration

body:
What is excretion?

Excretion is the biological process of removing metabolic waste substances produced by cells. Such wastes must be eliminated because their accumulation can disturb normal body functions.

Different organs remove different kinds of wastes. The lungs remove carbon dioxide and some water vapour. The kidneys remove dissolved nitrogenous wastes, excess water and certain salts by producing urine.

Where does urea come from?

Proteins in food are digested into amino acids, which the body uses for growth, repair and other functions. When amino acids are broken down, nitrogen-containing waste is produced. The liver converts much of this nitrogenous waste into urea, which is carried in the blood to the kidneys for removal.

Thus, the liver and kidneys have different but connected roles: the liver forms urea from nitrogenous waste, while the kidneys filter urea from the blood and eliminate it in urine.

Parts of the human urinary system

The human urinary system consists of 2 kidneys, 2 ureters, 1 urinary bladder and 1 urethra.

  • Kidneys: Filter the blood, remove dissolved wastes and regulate the amount of water and certain salts retained by the body.
  • Ureters: Carry urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder.
  • Urinary bladder: Temporarily stores urine.
  • Urethra: Carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.

The kidneys lie in the abdominal region, one on either side of the backbone. Blood reaches them through the renal arteries and returns towards the circulation through the renal veins.

Urine formation and elimination are separate events

Urine is formed in the kidneys. It then travels through the ureters and is stored in the bladder until urination. The bladder does not filter the blood or produce urine.

The kidneys help maintain the body's internal balance by adjusting how much water and certain dissolved substances are excreted. Urine output therefore varies with water intake, sweating and other conditions.

Excretion is different from egestion

When undigested food residues leave through the anus as faeces, the process is egestion. When metabolic wastes such as urea or carbon dioxide are removed, the process is excretion. Although both eliminate unwanted material, the materials have different origins.

Sweating removes water and salts and small quantities of certain wastes, but its major everyday function is cooling the body. It does not replace kidney function.

Prelims focus

  • The human urinary system has 2 kidneys, 2 ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
  • Urea is a major nitrogenous waste eliminated in human urine.
  • The liver forms urea from nitrogen-containing waste; the kidneys remove it from blood.
  • Ureters carry urine from kidneys to the bladder.
  • The urinary bladder stores urine; the urethra carries it outside.
  • Trap: The bladder stores urine but does not produce it.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.5.1, pp. 96–97, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, “Transportation in Animals and Plants”, pp. 126–128, 2018–19 printing.]

pictures.alt: Renal arteries bring blood to 2 kidneys and renal veins carry it away; urine flows through 2 ureters, 1 bladder and 1 urethra.
pictures.caption: Urine passes from the kidneys through ureters, bladder and urethra.

title: Human Excretion: Kidneys and the Urinary System

body:
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney

Each kidney contains a very large number of microscopic filtering units called nephrons. A nephron consists of a blood-filtering region and a long tubule in which useful substances can be recovered from the initial filtrate.

The filtering region contains a cluster of tiny blood capillaries called the glomerulus. It is surrounded by a cup-shaped structure called Bowman's capsule. The capsule collects fluid filtered from the blood.

How is urine formed?

1. Filtration at the glomerulus

Blood enters the glomerulus under pressure. Water and many small dissolved substances pass out of the blood and enter Bowman's capsule as glomerular filtrate. This initial filtrate contains useful substances as well as wastes.

Blood cells and most large blood proteins ordinarily remain within the blood vessels rather than entering the filtrate.

2. Selective reabsorption along the tubule

As filtrate passes through the nephron tubule, the body reabsorbs useful substances into the surrounding blood capillaries. These include glucose, amino acids, much of the water and selected salts.

Selective reabsorption is essential because the kidneys must remove wastes without losing all the useful substances that entered the initial filtrate. The amount of water reabsorbed depends partly on the body's water balance and the amount of waste that must be eliminated.

3. Collection and elimination of urine

The fluid remaining after filtration and reabsorption becomes urine. It passes into collecting ducts and through the kidney's urine-drainage pathways before entering the ureter. Urine then reaches the urinary bladder, where it is stored until urination.

Why is the amount of urine much smaller than the initial filtrate?

A healthy adult's kidneys may produce approximately 180 L of initial filtrate in 24 hours, while the urine finally passed is commonly only about 1–2 L in that period. These are approximate textbook figures, not fixed quantities for every person or situation.

The large difference occurs because most of the filtered water and many useful dissolved substances are reabsorbed. Actual urine volume varies with hydration, sweating, body conditions and kidney function.

How is dialysis related to kidney function?

If the kidneys fail to remove sufficient waste from the blood, harmful substances may accumulate. Dialysis can help remove dissolved wastes and excess water from the blood when kidney function is inadequate.

Dialysis performs an important waste-removal function, but it does not reproduce every function of a healthy kidney. In particular, its filtering process is not identical to the nephron's combination of filtration and selective tubular reabsorption.

How nutrition, respiration, circulation and excretion work together

The digestive system breaks food into absorbable nutrients. The respiratory system brings oxygen into the lungs. The circulatory system carries oxygen and nutrients to cells, where they support growth, repair and energy production.

Cells release carbon dioxide during aerobic respiration and also produce other metabolic wastes through their normal activities. Blood carries carbon dioxide towards the lungs and nitrogenous wastes towards the kidneys. The lungs eliminate carbon dioxide, and the kidneys remove urea and other substances in urine.

These relationships explain why no single life process can independently maintain a complex organism. Nutrition provides materials, respiration releases usable energy, circulation connects different organs, and excretion helps maintain a suitable internal environment.

Prelims focus

  • The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
  • The glomerulus filters blood; Bowman's capsule collects the initial filtrate.
  • Useful substances such as glucose, amino acids and much of the filtered water are selectively reabsorbed.
  • Urine contains dissolved wastes and water remaining after filtration and reabsorption.
  • Dialysis can remove wastes when kidney function is inadequate but does not fully reproduce normal nephron function.
  • Trap: Most initial filtrate is reabsorbed; it does not all become urine.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Sections 5.1, 5.3–5.5, pp. 80–81 and 87–98, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, “Transportation in Animals and Plants”, pp. 126–128, 2018–19 printing.]
